story.title: Ratko Mladic, Notorious Bosnian Serb War Criminal, Dies at 84
story.summary: Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb military leader convicted of genocide, has died at the age of 84 while serving a life sentence in a United Nations detention center in The Hague. Mladic was found guilty in 2017 for his role in the atrocities committed during the Bosnian War, including the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, which resulted in the deaths of at least 8,000 Muslims.

explore_lenses.label: What did the final verdict hold Mladić responsible for?
explore_lenses.title: Convictions covered a wider campaign
explore_lenses.summary: The final legal record went beyond Srebrenica: the UN tribunal found Mladić responsible for genocide there as well as crimes tied to ethnic cleansing, the siege of Sarajevo and the taking of UN personnel hostage.

claims.text: The ICTY convicted Mladić in November 2017 of genocide; crimes against humanity including persecution, extermination, murder, deportation and forcible transfer; and war crimes including terror, unlawful attacks on civilians and hostage-taking.
The Mechanism’s Appeals Chamber affirmed both the convictions and life sentence on June 8, 2021, making the judgment final.

The appeals judgment described four joint criminal enterprises, including permanently removing Bosnian Muslims and Croats from Bosnian Serb-claimed territory, terrorizing Sarajevo civilians, eliminating Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica, and taking UN personnel hostage.

explore_lenses.label: Why does Srebrenica remain central to this story?
explore_lenses.title: It was judicially established as genocide
explore_lenses.summary: Srebrenica is central because international courts found that the July 1995 killings and forced transfers constituted genocide, and Mladić was among the senior officials convicted for crimes there.

claims.text: After Bosnian Serb forces captured Srebrenica on July 11, 1995, up to 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys were killed or went missing, while about 30,000 women, children and elderly people were forcibly transferred, according to the UN.
The ICTY and International Court of Justice concluded that the acts committed at Srebrenica in 1995 constituted genocide.
Victims’ groups, including the Mothers of Srebrenica and Žepa Enclaves movement, said Mladić’s death should be understood through the crimes for which he was convicted and the victims left behind.

explore_lenses.label: What happens after his death in UN custody?
explore_lenses.title: Dutch procedures and a UN inquiry begin
explore_lenses.summary: Mladić died while hospitalized in The Hague, days after a court rejected his final request for conditional early release. The Mechanism says Dutch authorities are carrying out standard procedures and has ordered its own inquiry.

claims.text: The International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals said Mladić died while hospitalized in The Hague; Dutch authorities began the standard procedures and investigations required under Dutch law.
Mechanism President Judge Graciela Gatti Santana ordered a full inquiry into the circumstances of the death and assigned Judge Iain Bonomy to conduct it.

On August 20, the President denied Mladić’s request for conditional early release to a Serbian hospital or palliative-care facility, concluding that the care and family-contact arrangements available in The Hague did not make release necessary on humanitarian grounds.
At the time of his death, Mladić had been awaiting transfer to a state designated to enforce the remainder of his life sentence; that transfer will not occur.

story_report.summary: Ratko Mladić, the former Bosnian Serb military leader convicted of genocide and war crimes, died at 84 while in United Nations custody in The Hague. He had been serving a life sentence that became final in 2021. The International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals said he died while hospitalized; Dutch authorities began legally required procedures, and the Mechanism ordered a full inquiry into the circumstances of his death. A planned transfer to a state designated to enforce his sentence will no longer take place.

sections.heading: Srebrenica Genocide and Forced Displacement
sections.body: Bosnian Serb forces captured Srebrenica on July 11, 1995. The United Nations says that up to 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys were killed or went missing, while about 30,000 women, children and elderly people were forcibly transferred. The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and the International Court of Justice concluded that the acts committed there constituted genocide.

sections.heading: Mladić Convictions and Final Sentence
sections.body: The ICTY convicted Mladić in November 2017 of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. The convictions included persecution, extermination, murder, deportation, forcible transfer, terror, unlawful attacks on civilians and hostage-taking. The appeals judgment described joint criminal enterprises involving the permanent removal of Bosnian Muslims and Croats from Bosnian Serb-claimed territory, terrorizing Sarajevo civilians, eliminating Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica and taking UN personnel hostage; the Appeals Chamber upheld the convictions and life sentence in 2021.

sections.heading: Death Inquiry and Detention Procedures
sections.body: The Mechanism said Mladić had been awaiting transfer to a state designated to enforce the remainder of his life sentence. One week before his death, its president denied his request for conditional early release to a Serbian hospital or palliative-care facility, finding that treatment and family-contact arrangements in The Hague did not make humanitarian release necessary. Judge Iain Bonomy has been assigned to conduct the Mechanism’s inquiry.

unresolved.text: The findings of the Mechanism’s inquiry and the outcome of Dutch authorities’ procedures into Mladić’s death were not available as of August 27, 2026.

related_stories.title: Russian Serviceman Killed in St. Petersburg Car Explosion
related_stories.summary: A Russian military serviceman was killed in a car blast in St. Petersburg, marking the latest incident in a series of attacks targeting military personnel linked to Russia's involvement in the war against Ukraine. While Moscow often attributes such attacks to Ukraine, Kyiv has not consistently claimed responsibility.

related_stories.title: Trial Scheduled for Alleged 9/11 Mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed in 2028
related_stories.summary: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the alleged mastermind behind the September 11, 2001 attacks, is set to go on trial in June 2028. A US Air Force judge has ordered the trial to take place before a military tribunal at Guantanamo Bay, where Mohammed has been held since 2006. He is considered a high-ranking member of al-Qaeda and was captured in March 2003.

related_stories.title: King Harald's Health Declines as Family and Public Gather in Support
related_stories.summary: King Harald of Norway is reported to be in an 'extremely serious' condition in the hospital, prompting family members to gather at his bedside. As news of his health deteriorating spreads, hundreds of Norwegians have gathered outside the Royal Palace in Oslo, laying flowers in a show of support for the 89-year-old monarch.
